Q: How can I build multiple queries at once with CodeIgniter QueryBuilder? A:
  • Declare the shared clauses.
  • Count the unlimited, filtered rows without resetting the query builder (see the second parameter).
  • Fetch the calculated columns for the filtered, sorted, and limited rows.
  • When implementing a LIMIT, you must introduce an ORDER BY clause which ensures a deterministic result (databases do not guarantee any particular order by default).
$this->db
    ->from('table')
    ->where($reallyComplicated);

return [
    'total' => $this->db->count_all_results('', false),
    'rows' => $this->db
        ->select($calcFields)
        ->order_by($something)
        ->get('', 100)
        ->result()
];

Q: How can developers create UML diagrams, flowcharts, or swimlane diagrams to better visualize system workflows? A:

I will include a diagram in a design document when I think it helps illustrate what I'm trying to say.

UML has a specific "vocabulary" of design elements. Having those can help you keep your diagrams consistent, or you might find them too rigid or counterintuitive. Using UML or not is not unlike your choice of programming language, where if you're picking between say Rust and Go then both are fast modern compiled languages and your choice is probably based on something other than technical merits.

My experience here is a little colored by never having worked in a regulated industry with formal design and documentation requirements. You may be required to have specific documents with specific diagrams in specific formats, which will likely be UML.

In my current role, most things like engineering designs wind up in a wiki, and our particular wiki software allows writing Mermaid diagram markup directly in Markdown files. If I need a flowchart or an entity-relationship diagram, it'll show up in Mermaid format, because it's a tool I have very easy access to. It's not UML and that's fine.

Q: Which texture resolution to use (360/720/1080) when rendering every frame in OpenGL ES (Android) and Metal (iOS)? A:

I suspect you're worrying about performance problems that don't exist, at least from the GPU rendering point of view. Simple UI composition is something GPUs are very good at, so at least from a rendering point of view composing 2D layers at full native resolution is fine. Have you tried it and measured performance?

If you want sharp photos you want image texel size == screen pixel size. If you end up scaling down so it's smaller on screen then you'll want mipmaps and LINEAR_MIP_NEAREST filtering for quality reasons. (For a 2D viewer you shouldn't need LINEAR_MIP_LINEAR, which is more expensive).

Jitter issues are more likely to be on the software side (e.g. are you trying to upload new textures in the frame loop), and should be avoidable as complex games manage just fine ...

Q: Why does .net WCF Service require the Interface A:

injecting Interface, you can then use Service whatever you like in your class, without modifying your consuming class.

Nowadays (in NET.Core),

Injecting an interface is a foundational dependency injection (DI) technique where a class depends on an abstract contract (interface) rather than a concrete implementation. This promotes loose coupling, enhances testability, and allows swapping implementations at runtime without changing the consuming code. The container (InversionOfControl container) injects the specific implementation at startup.

If you really need creating this abstraction - you can benefit from it creating cross-platform applications. And you can benefit from Interface Segregation - if several developers are working on the project - you can also take any their implementations of the same class, injecting only Interface to your test-class, while being free to use any class, that implements it. So, injecting Dependency as abstraction your become less dependent on the implementation itself and can easy interchange it.

p.s. concerning Salesforce - good old ServiceContract can't be applied to SF. I was a little confused with conclusion here: "Don't use WCF listeners or ServiceModel, they exist for legacy mode and are not meant to be used moving forward." -- I think endpoint matters anyway.
